questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue and a sore tongue. Since her husband died she has lived on tea, toast and biscuits. She has pallor and a smooth red tongue. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 86 g/L (115–165), MCV 117 fL (80–100), platelets 162 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which type of anaemia is most likely?
questions.e: A poor diet with glossitis and an MCV over 100 means megaloblastic anaemia from impaired DNA synthesis (here likely folate deficiency).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which type of anaemia is most likely?
Poor diet, glossitis and a very high MCV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia from B12 or folate deficiency.

elim: Usually normocytic and needs a chronic inflammatory illness.
Gives jaundice and a high reticulocyte count; the MCV is not this high.
Gives a low MCV, not 117.
Rare and usually microcytic.

steps.x: D. Megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia. B12 or folate deficiency: megaloblastic anaemia with MCV above 100.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has 5 months of bloating, loose stools, weight loss and tiredness. Tissue transglutaminase antibodies are strongly positive. She has pallor and mouth ulcers. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165), MCV 106 fL (80–100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
questions.e: Coeliac disease damages the proximal small bowel and causes malabsorption of folate; anaemia without neurological signs fits folate deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?

clues: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies are strongly positive
steps.x: Malabsorption, macrocytosis and no neurology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Folate deficiency from coeliac malabsorption.

elim: Can raise the MCV slightly but does not fit coeliac malabsorption.
Common in coeliac disease but gives a low MCV.
Autoimmune gastritis in older women, usually with neurological features.
B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum, and there are no neurological signs.

steps.x: A. Folate deficiency. Folate deficiency: poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, malabsorption; no neurological signs.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman was diagnosed with pernicious anaemia 2 years ago and has hydroxocobalamin injections every 3 months. She feels well. She also has vitiligo. She asks whether her condition puts her at risk of any cancer. Her latest haemoglobin and MCV are normal.
questions.q: Which cancer is she at the greatest increased risk of?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune gastritis with intrinsic factor antibodies and predisposes to gastric carcinoma.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which cancer is she at the greatest increased risk of?
Pernicious anaemia attacks the stomach lining.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastric carcinoma.

elim: Not linked to pernicious anaemia.
Linked to cirrhosis and hepatitis B or C.
Linked to smoking and alcohol.
Not linked to autoimmune gastritis.

steps.x: B. Gastric carcinoma. Pernicious anaemia: intrinsic factor antibodies, autoimmune gastritis, raised gastric cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has 3 months of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. He has pallor and glossitis. Investigations: haemoglobin 92 g/L (130–180), MCV 112 fL (80–100). His GP needs to decide whether B12 or folate deficiency is more likely before results return.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most strongly suggest B12 rather than folate deficiency?
questions.e: Neurological symptoms with anaemia point to B12 deficiency; folate deficiency causes anaemia without neurology.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which additional finding would most strongly suggest B12 rather than folate deficiency?
Everything in the stem is shared by both deficiencies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neurological features separate B12 from folate deficiency.

elim: From anaemia, found in both.
Found in both.
Found in both.
From anaemia, found in both.

steps.x: E. Paraesthesia in both feet. Anaemia plus neurology = B12; anaemia alone could be either.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has 4 months of unsteadiness, especially walking in the dark, and tingling in his toes. He is pale. He has reduced vibration and joint position sense in both feet and Romberg's test is positive. Power is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 101 g/L (130–180), MCV 109 fL (80–100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sensory ataxia, loss of vibration sense and macrocytic anaemia together point specifically to B12 deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Dorsal column loss (worse in the dark, positive Romberg) with macrocytosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: B12 deficiency.

elim: Sudden onset with cerebellar signs and a negative Romberg's test.
Causes macrocytic anaemia without neurological signs.
Gait apraxia with urinary incontinence and confusion, not sensory loss or macrocytosis.
Tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia; no sensory loss.

steps.x: E. Vitamin B12 deficiency. B12 deficiency: neuropathy, loss of vibration sense, ataxia, plus macrocytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has Crohn's disease affecting only her terminal ileum, with no previous surgery. She has 3 months of fatigue and tingling fingers. Investigations: haemoglobin 97 g/L (115–165), MCV 111 fL (80–100), serum B12 low, folate normal. Her gastroenterologist explains why her Crohn's disease has caused this.
questions.q: Which part of the gut is responsible for absorbing the deficient vitamin?
questions.e: B12 is the only water-soluble vitamin absorbed in the terminal ileum, so ileal Crohn's (a malabsorption cause) leads to B12 deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which part of the gut is responsible for absorbing the deficient vitamin?
Low B12 with ileal disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Terminal ileum.

elim: The main site of iron absorption.
Intrinsic factor is made by parietal cells in the body and fundus, and absorption is not here.
The main site of folate absorption; her folate is normal.
Absorbs water, not vitamins.

steps.x: E. Terminal ileum. B12 is absorbed (bound to intrinsic factor) in the terminal ileum.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. She has 5 months of fatigue and numb feet. She eats meat and fish daily, drinks no alcohol, has normal bowel habit and takes only levothyroxine. Investigations: haemoglobin 89 g/L (115–165), MCV 115 fL (80–100), serum B12 74 ng/L (180–900), folate normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her B12 deficiency?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia is the most important cause of B12 deficiency, typically in middle-aged and older women with other autoimmune disease.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her B12 deficiency?

clues: She eats meat and fish daily
steps.x: Adequate diet, no malabsorption, autoimmune background.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pernicious anaemia.

elim: Normal bowel habit, and causes folate rather than B12 deficiency.
She eats meat and fish daily.
She takes only levothyroxine.
No bowel symptoms.

steps.x: D. Pernicious anaemia. Autoimmune woman + low B12 + normal diet = pernicious anaemia.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is 32 weeks pregnant with her third child in 4 years. She has tiredness and breathlessness. She eats very few vegetables. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 94 g/L (110–150), MCV 107 fL (80–100), ferritin normal, serum B12 normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
questions.e: Pregnancy and poor diet increase folate demand; macrocytosis without neurology with a normal B12 is folate deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
Pregnancy, closely spaced pregnancies and poor intake of leafy vegetables.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Folate deficiency.

elim: Ferritin is normal and the MCV is high.
A dilutional fall that is normocytic, not an MCV of 107.
Microcytic, not macrocytic.
Serum B12 is normal and there are no neurological signs.

steps.x: A. Folate deficiency. Pregnancy is a classic cause of folate deficiency.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has followed a strict vegan diet for 10 years and takes no supplements. He has macrocytic anaemia, a low serum B12 and early tingling in his feet. He is reluctant to start treatment because he feels only slightly tired. He asks what could happen if he does nothing.
questions.q: Which is the most important consequence of leaving his deficiency untreated?
questions.e: Untreated B12 deficiency causes permanent neurological damage (such as subacute combined degeneration) as well as ongoing anaemia and fatigue.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most important consequence of leaving his deficiency untreated?
Neurological symptoms have already started.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Irreversible neurological damage.

elim: Not a consequence of B12 deficiency.
Caused by repeated transfusion or haemochromatosis.
Not caused by B12 deficiency.
Not linked to B12 deficiency.

steps.x: D. Permanent neurological damage. Treat B12 deficiency promptly: neurological damage may become permanent.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man who drinks 70 units of alcohol a week has 3 months of fatigue. He has pallor and glossitis. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 95 g/L (130–180), MCV 113 fL (80–100), serum folate low, serum B12 normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
questions.e: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and nuclear maturation, giving oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (megaloblastic film).

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
Folate deficiency means megaloblastic change.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypersegmented neutrophils.

elim: Seen in acute myeloid leukaemia blasts.
The Pelger-Huët anomaly of myelodysplastic syndrome.
Seen in iron deficiency.
Seen in liver disease and thalassaemia; alcohol alone gives round macrocytes, not megaloblastic change.

steps.x: B. Hypersegmented neutrophils. Megaloblastic film: oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with a long history of anorexia nervosa has 2 months of tiredness, breathlessness and a sore mouth. Her BMI is 16 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Investigations: haemoglobin 91 g/L (115–165), MCV 109 fL (80–100), serum folate low. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her mouth?
questions.e: Glossitis (a smooth, red, sore tongue) is a feature of both B12 and folate deficiency along with fatigue, breathlessness and pallor.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her mouth?
Folate deficiency with oral symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glossitis.

elim: Linked to smoking, antibiotics and poor oral hygiene.
A benign patchy condition, not a deficiency sign.
White patches linked to smoking; premalignant.
Oral candidiasis.

steps.x: D. Smooth, red, painful tongue. Both deficiencies: fatigue, breathlessness, pallor, glossitis, MCV above 100.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman sees her GP with 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness on stairs. She has pallor and a smooth tongue. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her chest and heart sounds are normal. No blood tests have been done.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The FBC is the first-line test: a macrocytic anaemia prompts B12 and folate levels.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: No blood tests have been done
steps.x: Suspected anaemia with nothing done yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FBC first.

elim: Invasive and not a first-line test.
Not first-line; used later for specific concerns.
Used once B12 deficiency is shown, not first.
Useful later, but the FBC comes first in suspected anaemia.

steps.x: B. Full blood count. FBC first (macrocytic anaemia), then B12 and folate, then intrinsic factor antibodies.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with newly diagnosed pernicious anaemia is having hydroxocobalamin injections. Her anaemia has improved but she still has fatigue, weight gain, constipation and feels cold all the time. Her pulse rate is 56 bpm. Her haemoglobin is now 128 g/L (115–165).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia is linked to other autoimmune disease, especially hypothyroidism, which fits her fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

clues: weight gain, constipation and feels cold
steps.x: Hypothyroid features in a patient with an autoimmune condition.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check thyroid function.

elim: Her anaemia is responding; marrow is not needed.
No bowel symptoms suggesting cancer.
Already used to diagnose pernicious anaemia.
Levels are not used to monitor injections, and do not explain the new features.

steps.x: E. Thyroid function tests. Pernicious anaemia: look for associated autoimmune hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has a macrocytic anaemia and a serum B12 of 88 ng/L (180–900). She eats a normal diet and has no bowel symptoms. Gastric parietal cell antibodies are positive. Her haematologist wants the most specific test before labelling her with pernicious anaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Intrinsic factor antibodies are the most specific test for pernicious anaemia; parietal cell antibodies are less specific.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: Gastric parietal cell antibodies are positive
steps.x: The lead-in asks for specificity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intrinsic factor antibodies.

elim: Shows megaloblastic change but not its cause.
Sensitive but not specific; positive in many people without pernicious anaemia.
Raised in autoimmune gastritis but not specific.
Raised in both B12 and folate deficiency.

steps.x: B. Intrinsic factor antibodies. Intrinsic factor antibodies confirm pernicious anaemia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man drinks 35 units of alcohol a week and eats a limited diet. He has fatigue and mild glossitis. A full blood count shows haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180) and MCV 109 fL (80–100). His liver enzymes are mildly raised. He wants to know what is causing his anaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: Measuring B12 and folate is the gold standard test once the FBC shows macrocytic anaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
Macrocytic anaemia with poor diet and glossitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Measure B12 and folate.

elim: Assesses the liver but does not identify a vitamin deficiency.
Not needed before simple vitamin levels.
Supports alcohol excess but does not explain glossitis and anaemia.
Does not identify the cause of macrocytosis.

steps.x: E. Serum B12 and folate levels. Macrocytic anaemia on FBC: send serum B12 and folate.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has pernicious anaemia confirmed by positive intrinsic factor antibodies. Her haemoglobin is 92 g/L and serum B12 76 ng/L (180–900). Folate is normal. Neurological examination is normal. She is not breathless at rest.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks
questions.e: B12 deficiency is replaced with 1 mg hydroxocobalamin intramuscularly three times weekly initially; in pernicious anaemia oral absorption fails.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
B12 deficiency from pernicious anaemia without neurology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IM hydroxocobalamin loading doses.

elim: Folate is normal, and folic acid alone could mask B12 deficiency.
She has no iron deficiency.
A preconception dose, and she needs B12.
She is stable; the deficiency is easily replaced.

steps.x: A. IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks. B12 deficiency: 1 mg hydroxocobalamin three times weekly initially, then maintenance.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man who drinks 50 units of alcohol a week has fatigue and pallor. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 102 g/L (130–180), MCV 108 fL (80–100), serum B12 410 ng/L (180–900), serum folate 1.8 µg/L (3.0–20.0). He agrees to reduce his drinking.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral folic acid 5 mg once daily
questions.e: Folate deficiency is treated with 5 mg folic acid daily once B12 deficiency is excluded, with the cause (alcohol) addressed.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Isolated folate deficiency with a normal B12.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Folic acid 5 mg daily.

elim: His B12 is normal.
No iron deficiency.
The preconception dose, too low to treat deficiency.
Stable, with a treatable deficiency.

steps.x: D. Oral folic acid 5 mg once daily. Folate deficiency: 5 mg oral folic acid daily, and treat the cause.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with untreated coeliac disease has fatigue and tingling in her fingers. Investigations: haemoglobin 88 g/L (115–165), MCV 114 fL (80–100), serum B12 95 ng/L (180–900), serum folate 1.5 µg/L (3.0–20.0). She is haemodynamically stable.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Give folic acid alone and recheck in 4 weeks
Start B12 replacement before folic acid
Start folic acid first, then add B12
questions.e: In combined deficiency, treat B12 first to avoid precipitating subacute combined degeneration of the cord, then folate.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Both vitamins are low and she already has neurological symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: B12 first, then folate.

elim: Folate alone can mask the anaemia while the neuropathy worsens.
Needed long-term, but deficiencies must be replaced now.
She is stable.
The wrong order; it risks subacute combined degeneration.

steps.x: D. Start B12 replacement before folic acid. Combined B12 and folate deficiency: always replace B12 first.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has pernicious anaemia. He has completed 2 weeks of loading doses of intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and his symptoms have improved. Haemoglobin is now 121 g/L (130–180). He asks whether he can stop treatment now that he feels better.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Hydroxocobalamin injections every 3 months for life
Oral cyanocobalamin until the haemoglobin is normal
Repeat loading course only if symptoms return
Stop treatment and recheck B12 in a year
questions.e: When the absorption mechanism is permanently lost (pernicious anaemia, ileal resection), lifelong B12 replacement is needed.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
The cause is permanent loss of intrinsic factor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lifelong 3-monthly injections.

elim: Does not replace B12 and may mask deficiency.
He cannot absorb B12 without intrinsic factor, and treatment is not time-limited.
Neurological damage can occur before symptoms return.
The cause is permanent, so deficiency will recur.

steps.x: A. Hydroxocobalamin injections every 3 months for life. Pernicious anaemia or lost terminal ileum: lifelong B12 injections.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy has folate deficiency anaemia. Serum B12 is normal. She has no neurological symptoms. She has started folic acid 5 mg daily. She asks how to stop the deficiency coming back.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Long-term management treats the underlying cause: a gluten-free diet lets the gut heal so folate is absorbed again.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?

clues: coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy
how to stop the deficiency coming back
steps.x: The cause is malabsorption from coeliac disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the cause: gluten-free diet.

elim: Treats nothing and carries risk.
Her B12 is normal.
Not indicated without iron deficiency.
Used for strictures, not coeliac disease.

steps.x: E. Strict gluten-free diet. Long-term: treat the cause (diet, malabsorption, autoimmune disease).

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has followed a vegan diet for 6 years without supplements. She has mild tiredness. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations: haemoglobin 112 g/L (115–165), MCV 103 fL (80–100), serum B12 140 ng/L (180–900), folate normal. Intrinsic factor antibodies are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and recheck in a year
questions.e: Dietary B12 deficiency with normal absorption is treated with oral cyanocobalamin plus dietary advice; injections are needed when absorption fails or neurology is present.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: vegan diet for 6 years without supplements
steps.x: Dietary cause and normal absorption.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral cyanocobalamin with dietary advice.

elim: Folate is normal; it would not correct B12 deficiency.
No iron deficiency; the MCV is high.
Mild, stable anaemia.
B12 deficiency must be treated to prevent neurological damage.

steps.x: A. Oral cyanocobalamin. Vegan B12 deficiency: oral cyanocobalamin; pernicious anaemia: IM hydroxocobalamin.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has pernicious anaemia. Her serum folate is normal, yet her bone marrow shows megaloblastic change identical to that seen in folate deficiency. A medical student asks why lack of B12 produces the same blood picture as lack of folate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: B12 deficiency destroys erythroid stem cells
B12 deficiency increases red cell haemolysis in the spleen
B12 is a component of haem
B12 is needed to regenerate active folate for thymidine synthesis
B12 is required for iron absorption
questions.e: B12 and folate are both cofactors for DNA synthesis; B12 regenerates active folate, so without B12 folate becomes trapped and thymidine synthesis fails.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely explanation?
Normal folate, but folate-type marrow change.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: B12 is needed to keep folate in its active form.

elim: That is aplastic anaemia, not megaloblastic change.
Not the cause of megaloblastic change.
Haem contains iron, not cobalt.
Iron is absorbed in the duodenum independently of B12.

steps.x: D. B12 is needed to regenerate active folate for thymidine synthesis. B12 regenerates active folate; both are needed for thymidine (DNA) synthesis.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has megaloblastic anaemia from B12 deficiency. His bone marrow shows large erythroid precursors whose nuclei look immature compared with their well-haemoglobinised cytoplasm. His MCV is 119 fL (80–100) and the blood film shows oval macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils. A student asks why the red cells are so large.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the large red cells?
o: Delayed nuclear maturation with normal cytoplasmic development
Excess membrane lipid from liver disease
questions.e: Impaired DNA synthesis slows nuclear maturation while the cytoplasm keeps developing, so precursors keep growing: large, immature megaloblasts.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism for the large red cells?
The nucleus lags behind the cytoplasm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation.

elim: Gives round macrocytes and target cells, not megaloblasts.
Reticulocytes are larger but this is not megaloblastic change.
Iron does not enlarge red cells this way.
Gives small, pale (microcytic) cells.

steps.x: A. Delayed nuclear maturation with normal cytoplasmic development. Megaloblasts: nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony from impaired DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has macrocytic anaemia, loss of vibration sense in both legs and a positive Romberg's test. Serum B12 is low and serum methylmalonic acid is raised. His folate is normal. His consultant explains that the neurological damage comes from one B12-dependent enzyme that folate does not need.
questions.q: Which enzyme is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; its failure raises methylmalonic acid and disrupts myelin synthesis, causing neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which enzyme is most likely to be affected?
A raised methylmalonic acid names the enzyme.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

elim: The enzyme methotrexate inhibits; part of the folate cycle.
Deficiency causes oxidative haemolysis.
Thiamine-dependent.
Folate-dependent DNA synthesis enzyme, affected in both deficiencies.

steps.x: C. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. B12-only neurology = methylmalonyl-CoA mutase failure, raised MMA, defective myelin.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with pernicious anaemia asks why she cannot simply eat more meat and fish to correct her B12 deficiency. She eats a normal diet already. Her gastric parietal cell and intrinsic factor antibodies are both positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason that dietary B12 does not correct her deficiency?
o: Antibodies prevent intrinsic factor binding and absorbing B12
B12 is destroyed by gastric acid
Her bowel transit is too fast
Her kidneys excrete B12 too quickly
Meat and fish contain no B12
questions.e: Autoimmune antibodies target intrinsic factor or the parietal cells that make it, preventing B12 absorption despite adequate intake.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely reason that dietary B12 does not correct her deficiency?

clues: intrinsic factor antibodies are both positive
steps.x: Intake is fine; absorption is the problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No functioning intrinsic factor, so no absorption.

elim: B12 survives the stomach; she in fact has low acid.
No diarrhoea, and the problem is a missing carrier protein.
Renal loss is not the mechanism.
They are the main dietary sources.

steps.x: A. Antibodies prevent intrinsic factor binding and absorbing B12. Pernicious anaemia: no intrinsic factor, no B12 absorption, so give it by injection.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman was given folic acid 5 mg daily for macrocytic anaemia without B12 being checked. After 2 months her haemoglobin has risen from 90 to 122 g/L, but she now has numb legs and an unsteady gait. Her serum B12 is 60 ng/L (180–900).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her worsening neurology?
o: Folic acid directly damages the dorsal columns
Folic acid restored DNA synthesis while the B12-dependent myelin defect progressed
Spinal cord compression from a new metastasis
Stroke caused by the rise in haemoglobin
questions.e: Folic acid alone fuels DNA synthesis via the folate pathway and masks the anaemia, while B12-dependent myelin damage continues unchecked.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her worsening neurology?

clues: numb legs and an unsteady gait
steps.x: The blood got better and the nerves got worse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Masking: folate corrects anaemia, not the B12 neurological defect.

elim: Folate is not neurotoxic.
No link, and her haemoglobin rose.
No cancer history; the timing fits B12 deficiency.
Symmetrical sensory leg signs do not fit stroke.

steps.x: C. Folic acid restored DNA synthesis while the B12-dependent myelin defect progressed. Never give folic acid alone in possible B12 deficiency: it masks the anaemia.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had a terminal ileal resection with an ileostomy for Crohn's disease 5 years ago. She stopped her 3-monthly hydroxocobalamin injections 2 years ago because she felt well. She now has 3 months of fatigue and breathlessness. Investigations: haemoglobin 90 g/L (115–165), MCV 116 fL (80–100).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Without a terminal ileum she cannot absorb B12, so stopping injections leads to recurrent deficiency with ongoing anaemia and fatigue.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
Lost absorption site and stopped replacement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: B12 deficiency has returned.

elim: Usually normocytic; her MCV is 116.
Folate is absorbed in the jejunum, which is intact.
Would give a low MCV.
Causes diarrhoea and dehydration, not macrocytosis on its own.

steps.x: D. Recurrent vitamin B12 deficiency. Lost terminal ileum = lifelong B12; stopping it brings back anaemia and fatigue.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has 6 months of burning and numbness in both feet and unsteadiness. He has no diabetes and drinks little alcohol. He has reduced vibration sense to the knees and absent ankle reflexes. Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L (130–180), MCV 106 fL (80–100), HbA1c normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Neurological symptoms with a raised MCV point to B12 deficiency; serum B12 and folate is the diagnostic test.

steps.x: The lead-in asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Neuropathy, raised MCV and diabetes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check B12 and folate.

elim: Does not assess a symmetrical peripheral sensory neuropathy.
Not a first test for a chronic sensory neuropathy.
May be needed later, but a simple blood test comes first.
Characterise the neuropathy but do not identify a treatable cause.

steps.x: E. Serum B12 and folate. Neuropathy plus macrocytosis: send serum B12 and folate.
